Shocking stat of the day:

Estimated annualized interest expense on US federal debt is up to a record $1.38 trillion.

This is equivalent to 4.2% of US GDP, the highest percentage since 1997.

By comparison, this figure stood at 2.3% in Q4 2020.

Annualized interest expense has surged +$900 billion, or nearly +200%, over the last 5 years, rising at an average annual rate of +24%.

Meanwhile, in the first 9 months of FY2026, interest expense jumped +$78 billion YoY, to $827 billion, the highest level for this period in history.

The cost of servicing US federal debt has never been higher.

Employment in the US financial industry is going through a prolonged downturn:

The financial industry shed -14,000 jobs in July, to 9.09 million, the lowest since July 2022.

This marks the 5th consecutive monthly decline, totaling -59,000.

Since May 2025, financial industry payrolls have dropped -121,000, posting the largest drawdown since the 2020 pandemic.

Excluding the pandemic, this is the biggest employment contraction in the sector since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

The decline comes as financial firms accelerate AI adoption, aiming to boost productivity and reduce labor costs across the industry.

AI is reshaping the future of employment in finance.

Institutional investors are dumping US tech equities:

Hedge funds, asset managers, and other institutional investors sold -$21.6 billion of Nasdaq futures during the week ending August 4th, the largest weekly sale on record, according to Goldman Sachs.

Short sales dominated the move, accounting for 72% of total sales.

Hedge funds sold -$11.9 billion over this period while asset managers sold -$7.4 billion.

As a result, combined institutional investor positioning in Nasdaq futures fell to -$5 billion, turning negative for the first time since May 2025.

By comparison, this figure was as high as +$54 billion in October 2025.

Institutional investors are selling into market strength.

Leveraged ETFs are now driving markets.

Leveraged ETFs now account for a record 16% of total global ETF daily trading value.

This is despite representing only ~$250 billion, or 1%, of the total ~$22 trillion global ETF industry.

This comes as 30-day average trading volume in leveraged ETFs has tripled since January, to a record ~$70 billion in June.

Furthermore, long-leveraged ETFs are seeing ~$43 billion in average daily turnover, compared to ~$18 billion in short-leveraged funds.

Meanwhile, AI-related long-leveraged ETFs now account for a record 58% of total exposure across long-leveraged ETFs, up from 26% in 2022.

Among single-stock long-leveraged ETFs, memory stocks alone account for 48% of total exposure.

This market is seeing massive amounts of leverage.

US business insurance prices just fell for the first time in 9 years.

Commercial property and casualty premiums dropped -1.2% in Q1 2026.

This officially ends a 33-quarter run of increases and marks the first decline since Q3 2017.

Since 2017, total US property and casualty net premiums written have risen from ~$560 billion to ~$980 billion.

In other words, despite the decline, US property and casualty insurance premiums are still up +74% since 2017.

Insurance premiums remain a major source of cost pressure on US businesses despite the recent reversal.

BREAKING: US household debt fell -$13 billion in Q2 2026, to $18.77 trillion, the 3rd-highest level on record.

This marks the first quarterly decline since the 2020 pandemic.

However, since the end of 2019, total household debt has surged +$4.63 trillion.

The Q2 decrease was driven by mortgage debt, which fell -$74 billion, to $13.12 trillion.

At the same time, student loan balances declined -$7 billion, to $1.65 trillion, the lowest since Q2 2025.

Meanwhile, credit card debt rose +$21 billion, to $1.26 trillion, the 2nd-highest on record.

Auto loans jumped +$28 billion, to $1.71 trillion, an all-time high.

Are American households approaching their debt limit?
